articles.title: Spain’s Parliament backs citizenship for Western Saharans born before 1977
articles.summary: After lower house approval, the bill to grant tens of thousands of Sahrawis citizenship now goes to the Spanish Senate.
articles.body:
Spanish lawmakers have backed legislation that would grant citizenship to tens of thousands of Western Saharans who were born when Spain ran the disputed territory now largely controlled by Morocco.

Spain’s lower house of Parliament on Thursday approved the legislation 168-31, with 145 abstentions.

The bill still requires Senate approval before becoming law.

The text grants Spanish nationality to Sahrawis born before September 29, 1977 and to their children through naturalisation, even if they never resided in Spain.

Although the exact number of beneficiaries is unknown, Sahrawi groups estimate that between 70,000 and 120,000 people could benefit from the legislation, which supporters described as addressing a “historical injustice” by colonial Spain in the Western Sahara.

The vote comes at a particularly sensitive time for Madrid’s historically delicate relations with Rabat due to the migration crisis in Spain’s north African territory of Ceuta, and the mass arrival of at least 70,000 migrants from Morocco in July.

Spain’s leftist government has avoided blaming Morocco – which does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over Ceuta and Spain’s other North African territory of Melilla – but the right accuses Rabat of orchestrating the surge for political motives.

Morocco claims sovereignty over Western Sahara and began asserting control over the territory after Spanish ⁠rule ended.

The Algerian-backed Polisario Front independence movement seeks recognition ⁠of an independent state called the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic.

Many Sahrawis live in refugee camps in Tindouf in western Algeria, or elsewhere abroad, while others remain in Western Sahara.

Against this backdrop, the initiative to grant Spanish nationality to Sahrawis has divided opinion in Morocco but not prompted condemnation from the government.

Moroccan media quoted Ramadan Messaoud, a member of the Royal Advisory Council for Saharan Affairs, as saying in July that Rabat had “no problem” with Sahrawis obtaining Spanish citizenship. Others had done so “over the past few years”, noted Messaoud, who is also president of the Sahrawi Association for Human Rights.

Western Sahara was a Spanish colony until 1975, when Spain relinquished its administration under agreements with Morocco and Mauritania.

Spain’s ruling Socialist Party and its junior left-wing partner Sumar, which filed the initiative, were among those who supported the bill, ‌while the opposition conservative People’s Party abstained and far-right Vox voted against it.

“With the adoption of this legislation, we are restoring – and I emphasise, restoring – the Spanish national identity card to those Sahrawis who once held it and from whom this state took it away,” said Tesh Sidi of the leftist Sumar coalition, the first woman of Sahrawi origin ⁠to serve in Spain’s Parliament.

The bill will now go to the Senate, where amendments are expected, before returning to the lower house for final approval.

articles.title: Prosecutor who led ‘grand conspiracy’ probe of Trump targets resigns without charging anyone
articles.summary: Joe diGenova, 81, was part of a group that tried to overturn the 2020 election.
articles.body: Joe diGenova, the 81-year-old Trump loyalist who had headed a sprawling investigation in the Southern District of Florida that targeted President Donald Trump’s perceived political enemies, has resigned from the Justice Department. “It was an honor and a privilege to serve the president and the department,” diGenova said Thursday. Asked why he is leaving, diGenova declined to comment. “I’m moving on,” he said. ABC News first reported diGenova’s departure. While diGenova resigned from the Justice Department and was not fired, a source familiar with the determination told NBC News that Justice Department officials had already lost confidence in his leadership skills and his ability to run the investigation. Justice Department leadership felt the investigation was not moving quickly enough, even though diGenova was provided with a team of Justice Department lawyers from Washington, according to the source familiar with the determination, who said the hope is the probe can get back on track with those attorneys at the helm. For now, a specific person will not be named to take diGenova’s place, and the investigation is expected to move forward without delays. The Justice Department declined to comment on diGenova’s resignation. DiGenova, a top federal prosecutor under President Ronald Reagan, was part of Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election in his favor. He made headlines this year when it was revealed that he would head the Florida-based investigation into Trump’s foes. DiGenova’s probe has not produced any prosecutions, though shortly before he resigned there was a recent burst of activity in the wide investigation. The Justice Department is seeking testimony from multiple former officials before a federal grand jury, people familiar with the probe told NBC News. The Associated Press first reported the subpoena activity. The probe reached back a decade, revisiting a Justice Department inquiry into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election. That posed a major hurdle for the investigation, given that the activity took place nearly a decade ago, far outside the typical five-year statute of limitations for most federal crimes. DiGenova stepped in to replace career prosecutor Maria Medetis Long, who had objected to advancing an investigation into former CIA Director John Brennan, whom Trump allies were pushing to be charged for allegedly false testimony. The grand conspiracy investigation was taking place in a legal district that has historically been advantageous for Trump, overseen by the Trump-appointed U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, Jason A. Reding Quiñones, and using a grand jury in a Fort Pierce court run by U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, a Trump-friendly judge. Then-acting Attorney General Todd Blanche appointed diGenova in April, shortly after Pam Bondi was fired. DiGenova, joined by his wife, Victoria Toensing, whom he brought into his team along with Rudy Giuliani and Sidney Powell, was part of a group that repeatedly tried and failed to overturn Trump’s 2020 election loss.

articles.title: Fatwas, holy wars and socialism: Inside the Islamic conference where El-Sayed drew a hero’s welcome
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed headlined an ISNA conference where an attendee called for a fatwa against members of Congress.
articles.body: DETROIT, Mich. — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed headlined an Islamic conference over Labor Day weekend where the United States was described as an empire in decline, early Islamic conquests were praised and the aftermath of 9/11 was framed around Islamophobia and discrimination. The event, held annually by the Islamic Society of North America, featured a range of speakers discussing topics from Muslim civic participation to the ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas. Over the course of the conference’s speeches and panel discussions, participants took positions that were generally critical of the United States and the broader Western world and expressed opinions that some may regard as extreme. EXILED MUSLIM SCHOLAR WARNS FAR-LEFT–ISLAMIST ALLIANCE BEHIND ANTI-ISRAEL PROTESTS ECHOES IRAN’S RISE Fox News Digital attended the event over the weekend, sitting in on many of the panels held on Saturday and Sunday before and after El-Sayed's speech. The Michigan Democrat is running in one of the most hotly contested Senate races of the 2026 cycle, the outcome of which may decide control of the Senate. At one panel, "Rising Islamophobia in the U.S.," a speaker described recently passed legislation that could bar colleges participating in certain commercial boycotts of Israel from receiving some federal higher education funds as "an anti-Muslim bill." Shortly after that, a man in the audience wearing a Pakistani flag pin stood up and called for a fatwa to be issued against the bipartisan group of lawmakers who voted for the bill. A fatwa is a religious ruling or opinion that can range from a formal condemnation to, in some cases, a call for or justification of violence. The legislation was introduced by Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., and co-sponsored by Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J. After the man called for a fatwa against members of Congress, members of the audience — and one panelist — applauded. Earlier, during the same discussion, a panelist criticized Congress for moving to censure Reps. Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib for making "​​the most lighthearted comments" Tlaib was censured in part for endorsing the phrase "from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free," which calls for the destruction of Israel as bounded by the Jordan River in the east and the Mediterranean Sea in the west. Critics characterized the phrase as a call for ethnic cleansing, while the congresswoman defended it as "an aspirational call for freedom, human rights and peaceful coexistence." ISNA is a nonprofit Muslim religious organization established in 1981 to provide America's growing Muslim population with a platform for civic coordination and education. Detroit, where the event took place, is situated in a metropolitan area that has a significant Arab American population concentrated in areas such as Dearborn and Hamtramck. EL-SAYED CAMPAIGN BACKED BY OVER $100,000 FROM DOZENS OF MEMBERS OF GROUP WITH ALLEGED TERROR TIES Panelists also accused billionaire Elon Musk of funding a White supremacist global anti-Muslim movement, suggested that some of the narrative regarding 9/11 taught in American schools has been "debunked" and asserted that Muslims were treated unfairly in the wake of the 2001 attacks. Criticism of America’s response to 9/11 surfaced repeatedly across the conference’s events and breakout sessions. One speaker asserted that one of the most important things to reflect on as the 25th anniversary of 9/11 approaches is that "Islamophobia is at an all-time high." Another called the War on Terror, a series of post-9/11 military operations that claimed the lives of over 7,000 U.S. military personnel, the "War of Terror." El-Sayed has sought to moderate his public image since launching his Senate campaign, even as he has maintained ties to prominent socialists and socialist-aligned activists. His attendance at the recent ISNA conference is the latest in a series of associations that have drawn criticism, including ties to Nation of Islam figures, Muslim clerics accused of expressing support for terrorist organizations and activists on the socialist left. In response to these charges, the Democrat has pointed out that GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers has links to individuals who echo conspiracy theories about the 2020 election or who have called for bans on gay marriage. EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS Before the event, El-Sayed’s campaign moved to distance the candidate from other conference speakers. "Abdul is not affiliated with and does not endorse any other participant of the conference," a spokeswoman for his campaign told media outlets in the lead-up to the event. The statement followed reports that he would appear alongside Islamic clerics who defended child marriage and praised U.S.-designated terrorist organizations, including al Qaeda. Of the controversial speakers, only the cleric who had defended child marriage was ultimately disinvited, The Washington Free Beacon previously reported. ISNA appeared to anticipate scrutiny over some of the speakers it invited to the conference. In the conference venue’s main hallway, the organization posted a prominent sign which says, "ISNA does not endorse the actions of convention participants and explicitly disclaims any responsibility for the views expressed, information provided, or materials displayed, sold or distributed by convention speakers, performers, exhibitors, vendors, or attendees." COUNTERTERRORISM EXPERT WARNS ABDUL EL-SAYED SENATE BID RAISES HOMELAND SECURITY CONCERNS While ISNA sought to distance itself from the controversial views expressed by some conference speakers, the organization itself took actions that also drew scrutiny. Fox News Digital spoke to three Christian evangelists outside the conference who claimed they were removed from it without warning. Each of them said they were simply having conversations with individuals who wanted to speak with them before they were escorted outside by security. Attendance at the conference was open to people of all faiths, and registration did not require attendees to be Muslim. The conference also held an interfaith banquet on Sunday. The disclaimer took on added significance in light of books available for purchase at the conference’s on-site bazaar. Fox News Digital found books that defended Islamic warfare while portraying Christianity as uniquely violent. "Christians are the last people on earth who should bring the charge of bloodshed and cruelty against followers of any other system, for it is a well-established fact that no religion known to history has such a horrible sanguinary record as church Christianity," one book sold at the conference reads. Another book argued that all Islamic warfare is defensive, defended non-Muslims being forced to pay a discriminatory tax and claimed that Christian civilization has killed nearly 200 million people by attributing wars that did not have religious motivations or were not initiated by Christians. The French Revolution, which was instigated by individuals hostile to Christianity, for instance, is counted toward Christianity’s death count. The Korean War, which was launched by communist North Korea, is also counted toward the body count of Christianity. UNEARTHED INTERVIEW REVEALS EL-SAYED’S SHARIA ‘OBLIGATION’: ‘NOT BECAUSE OF FEAR’ The conference also featured advertisements for "Sharia-compliant" mortgages and other financial products. El-Sayed held a quasi-celebrity status among the conference’s attendees. Campaign buttons were nearly ubiquitous at the conference, and his campaign’s booth was easily the busiest of those located in the main hall, Fox News Digital found. When the Senate hopeful walked on stage to address the conference, he was greeted with a thunderous standing ovation. Calls of "we love you" rang out from the crowd. El-Sayed’s speech was ultimately measured and largely focused on unity, representation and the idea that Muslim and American identities are compatible. "As we leave here tonight, I’ve got a challenge for each and every one of you," El-Sayed said with a measured cadence reminiscent of former President Barack Obama. "It’s the question of how you show up in the spaces in which you show up everyday, as wholly and 100% yourself. Because we are a community as Muslim Americans who believe in the rhyming of our Muslim ideals and our American ideals. That those two things are not mutually exclusive, in fact, that at their best being Muslim makes us better Americans and being Muslim enables us to be better Americans." ‘DESTROYING THE AMERICAN WAY OF LIFE’: EL-SAYED’S POLITICAL ORBIT COMPLICATES EFFORT TO MODERATE HIS IMAGE But elsewhere at the conference, speakers offered a markedly different assessment of America and its place in the world. "The world has become multipolar, and we see almost like the fear and insecurity that the empire has at this moment if we think through the lens of the U.S. So, I like to think that we are on the very end of an ending empire," an academic speaking at a session about the conflict between Israel and Hamas said. "I'm very positive about it." The same panelist later argued that referring to the river next to Detroit as the "Detroit River" was an immoral act of colonialism because Native Americans had a different name for the waterway. In a similar vein, a speaker at one of the conference’s main sessions criticized American foreign policy after the 9/11 terrorist attacks, then credited the "TikTok generation" with mobilizing in favor of Palestinians following the Oct. 7 terrorist attacks. Some speakers, however, made a clear effort to connect El-Sayed’s socialist project with his Islamic faith. "Islam historically was not just spread by the instance of Dawah. It was spread by socialism," said a cleric who would go on to speak positively about early Islamic conquests. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP ISNA declined comment. The El-Sayed campaign did not respond to requests for comment after being reached by Fox News Digital Wednesday.

articles.title: Bioweapon threat exposed as Anthropic sounds alarm on foreign actors plotting virus experiments
articles.summary: Researchers outside the United States used Anthropic's Claude to plan gain-of-function experiments on bird flu, chikungunya and dangerous toxins.
articles.body: Researchers outside the United States used frontier AI models to plan experiments involving highly pathogenic bird flu, chikungunya and other biological agents with potential weapons applications, according to a new threat report from Anthropic. The researchers used AI to study viruses’ transmissibility and immune evasion, investigate orthopoxvirus immune-response genes and help design novel toxins at times while taking steps to evade safeguards meant to restrict access to dangerous biological capabilities. Anthropic detailed five cases in the report published Thursday but withheld the countries, institutions and specific biological agents involved. The company stressed that it is not claiming the researchers intended to develop biological weapons. AI KILL SWITCH BILL COULD SHUT DOWN ROGUE MODELS The findings offer a concrete glimpse at a threat that has largely been discussed in hypothetical terms. Scientists who already possess biological expertise, materials and laboratory access are using increasingly powerful AI systems to accelerate sensitive dual-use research. They also land amid a renewed debate over catastrophic AI risks. Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher, recently resigned while accusing the companies of "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." His warning drew more than 100 million views on X. SEN BERNIE SANDERS: YES, WE MUST HIT THE PAUSE BUTTON ON AI BEFORE IT IS TOO LATE Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s alignment science lead, separately said he personally believed there was a greater than 10% chance AI could kill all humans within the next decade. But Anthropic’s report points to a threat that is already taking shape: researchers using frontier AI for potentially dangerous biological work, circumventing geographic restrictions and adapting when the models’ safeguards get in their way. In one case, Anthropic blocked a grant application for chikungunya gain-of-function research at a military research institute. The proposed work focused on identifying mutations that could increase the virus’s transmissibility and ability to evade the immune system. The researchers planned to engineer those mutations into infectious clones and repeatedly pass the virus through live animals, selecting for variants that caused the most severe disease. That work could help scientists develop better vaccines and treatments for chikungunya. It could also produce a more dangerous pathogen that would be difficult to distinguish from a naturally occurring outbreak, Anthropic said. The researchers accessed Claude through a life sciences platform that tunneled traffic through U.S. infrastructure to evade Anthropic’s regional restrictions. When Claude refused to answer sensitive prompts, the platform routed those requests to another model with more permissive safeguards. Anthropic said the research continued after the company banned accounts connected to the activity. The platform operator reestablished access within days using new identities, while Claude continued to provide editorial assistance on research materials. In another case, a researcher spent weeks using Claude to plan experiments involving mammalian adaptation and airborne transmission in highly pathogenic avian influenza. FDA APPROVES FIRST-EVER MRNA FLU VACCINE FOR MILLIONS OF OLDER AMERICANS The researcher was studying viral traits that could allow bird flu to spread more effectively among mammals and cause severe disease outside the respiratory system. A version capable of efficient human-to-human transmission would pose a significant pandemic threat, according to the report. Anthropic said the researcher appeared to have access to virus isolates and animal-model facilities. The company confined the work to weaker models, limiting the assistance primarily to study design, data analysis and editorial support. The company said the case provided evidence of an active research program developing the knowledge and biological materials needed to create pathogens with enhanced pandemic potential. The researcher also took steps to hide his identity while accessing the models from an unsupported region. A separate user connected to a state-associated infectious-disease laboratory used Claude to draft an orthopoxvirus research grant from start to finish in about an hour. Orthopoxviruses include variola, the virus that causes smallpox, as well as mpox. The grant application proposed studying viral genes that disable the human immune response and included the central hypothesis, experimental design, dosing, statistical plans and contingency strategies. Because the work was framed around weakening the virus, Claude’s safeguards did not block the assistance. But Anthropic said the same knowledge could also help a researcher preserve or enhance the virus’ immune-evasion capabilities. The final two cases involved venom peptides and toxins. One researcher used Claude to build an atlas of toxin peptides from multiple venomous animal lineages and then created a generative pipeline to optimize their characteristics. The stated goal was to develop new painkillers, antidepressants and other treatments. But the atlas also included structures associated with paralytic toxins that could potentially be used as incapacitating agents. Anthropic said the work was part of a state-supported research program. In the other case, a researcher used Claude to computationally redesign several toxins, including a bacterial toxin and a protein from a hemorrhagic fever virus identified by the World Health Organization as a priority disease threat. The researcher used Claude to help prepare progress reports but instructed the model to keep the identities of the toxins deliberately vague. The cases illustrate why biological misuse can be difficult to prevent through automated filters alone. Anthropic’s safeguards blocked the clearest attempts involving enhanced pandemic pathogens, but they were less effective when users framed their work as medical, defensive or therapeutic research. "Biological capabilities are dual use," Anthropic said in the report. "The same information that can be used to develop a biological weapon could also be used to develop, for example, a vaccine or a cure for a disease." The company said it recently reviewed 30 days of activity associated with adversarial state institutions and found roughly 35 distinct biological research efforts. Most involved ordinary civilian science, but some had "notable dual-use potential." Anthropic said the findings do not show that Claude has enabled an imminent biological attack. They do show, the company said, that researchers tied to state-associated programs are attempting to evade access controls and use frontier AI models in biological research that could have weapons applications. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The company said future safeguards will likely require more than content filters, including identity verification, institutional vetting and closer monitoring of users seeking access to advanced biological capabilities.

articles.title: Donald Trump joins well-trodden presidential path to the Emerald Isle
articles.summary: In recent decades, Ireland has become a particularly frequent fixture for US presidential trips.
articles.body:
When Donald Trump lands in Dublin on Saturday, he will be on a well-trodden international path.

In recent decades, Ireland has become a particularly frequent fixture for US presidential trips.

It stands out among small countries as hosting a high number of visits.

The bond between the two nations was forged by emigration, deepened by economic ties, and cemented by the Northern Ireland peace process – in which Washington played a major role.

Historians generally estimate that around five million people left Ireland for the US in the 19th and early 20th centuries.

Dr Peter McLoughlin, who teaches history and politics at Queen's University Belfast, said that created an "enormous ethnic link".

In 2024, census data found that 32.4 million Americans claimed Irish ancestry – almost one in ten of the population.

That means several presidents have seen political advantage in being seen to explore their heritage.

John F Kennedy was the first president to go to Ireland while in office.

In June 1963, he visited his ancestral homestead in County Wexford, from where his great-grandfather had left during the Irish potato famine in 1848.

In his address to the Irish Parliament, he said: "This has never been a rich or powerful country, and yet, since earliest times, its influence on the world has been rich and powerful."

In the years since, Ireland has become rich by many global measures, with some of the US's biggest firms driving its economic growth.

Tech and pharmaceutical firms - such as Apple, Pfizer and Meta - have key European bases in Ireland.

The rapid expansion of US investment in Ireland in the 1990s coincided with the development of the peace process in Northern Ireland.

Bill Clinton's three visits to the island took in both sides of the border , and he was strongly involved in the Good Friday Agreement in 1998, which largely ended the conflict in Northern Ireland after three decades.

McLoughlin, who has researched America's role, said: "It's one of the examples where you can see US power being used in a successful way to get a peaceful settlement.

"After Clinton, George W Bush was maybe not such a hands-on president as regards Northern Ireland, but his White House was important in making sure the Good Friday Agreement was implemented."

Politicians, civic leaders and business figures from Belfast and Dublin are hosted in Washington each year on Ireland's national holiday, St Patrick's Day.

The taoiseach (Irish prime minister) traditionally presents the president with a bowl of shamrock, the plant which is a symbol of Ireland.

Dan Mulhall, who was Ireland's Ambassador to Washington from 2017-22, said the yearly access to the White House was "pretty unique".

"I remember some of my European colleagues were kind of puzzled as to how Ireland had pulled this off, given that some of them also have large diaspora communities in the US, but they don't seem to have the same impact or lasting connection with their ancestral homeland as the Irish Americans undoubtedly have."

Barack Obama paid homage to his heritage in 2011 , when he visited his great-great-great grandfather's home village of Moneygall in County Offaly.

In a speech in Dublin, he joked: "I've come home to find the apostrophe that we lost somewhere along the way."

Joe Biden described Ireland as "part of his soul" on his trip in 2023 , which was the last US presidential visit.

He went to his ancestral counties of Mayo and Louth and marked the 25th anniversary of the Good Friday Agreement.

Donald Trump's visit will be different in content and tone.

His focus will be on golf rather than genealogy, as he will watch the Irish Open played at his resort in Doonbeg in County Clare.

In Dublin, he will meet the Taoiseach Micheàl Martin and the Irish President Catherine Connolly.

Connolly has a largely ceremonial role as head-of-state, but she has previously been a staunch critic of US foreign policy, particularly in the Middle East.

Earlier this year Trump referred to Connolly as "he" when responding to criticisms she made about the US attack on Iran being "a brutal assault on international law".

The US Embassy in Dublin criticised a law passed by the Irish Parliament this year to ban the importation of goods from Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territory.

The Embassy said the legislation "risked real unintended consequences, particularly for nearly 1000 US companies and the hundreds of thousands of Irish jobs tied to them".

US actions abroad will be the focus of protests in Dublin and County Clare this weekend.

On Thursday a large sand artwork appeared on a beach in Dublin Bay.

The campaign group Uplift carved the words 'No kings - Gaza Iran Ice' into the sand.

Washington's trade policy has been another prominent issue in Ireland, as Trump has expressed unhappiness at the scale of US pharmaceutical manufacturing in the country.

However, tariffs have mostly not been imposed on the sector.

Mullhall, the former Ireland Ambassador to Washington said the economic relationship was "as strong as it's ever been".

He thinks the Irish government will approach Trump's visit with "prudent realism".

"It's not possible to expect that a small country, any country in fact, can deflect Donald Trump from any of his purposes or policies.

"Most countries have adopted the strategy of simply trying to ride out the Trump term and hope for more predictable days ahead.

"So I think the government will play it safe and will be above all else, be wanting to avoid any kind of tension or difficulty between themselves and Donald Trump."

McLoughlin, of Queen's University, sees parallels between Trump's visit and that of Ronald Reagan in 1984, when there was opposition over US foreign policy in Latin America.

The Catholic church was very influential in Ireland at that time and McLoughlin pointed out that senior clergy did not meet Reagan.

"This was a time when many people would have members of the family who were in Latin America as a nun or a priest, and were bringing back first-hand reports of how there were controversial associations with US policy, with right-wing paramilitaries who were engaged in the Cold War struggle."

But he said that amidst the criticism of the visit, the Irish government wanted to "court" Reagan, for "economic reasons, and political reasons involving Northern Ireland".

He added that pictures of Reagan exploring his ancestry, in County Tipperary, helped make the visit "successful" from Dublin and Washington's point of view.

Ireland is more used than most countries to hosting the holder of the most powerful office in the world and the diplomatic delicacies around Trump's visit are another episode in a story dating back many decades.

articles.title: Jimmy Kimmel says interview with Democrat James Talarico won't air on TV
articles.summary: The White House denies Kimmel's allegations regarding his interview with James Talarico, accusing the TV host of "play acting".
articles.body:
TV host Jimmy Kimmel says his interview with Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico will not air on television due to pressure from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC).

Speaking on his talk show, Jimmy Kimmel Live!, on Wednesday, Kimmel said the FCC, under Donald Trump's presidency, had threatened him and his show "based on simple traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don't like". The BBC has contacted the FCC for comment.

A White House spokesman denied the head of the FCC had threatened Kimmel regarding his interview with Talarico or any other candidate.

Trump-backed Republican Ken Paxton will face Talarico in November's midterm elections.

The outcome of the Texas race will help determine whether Democrats can win back control of the US Senate for the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency.

During his show on Wednesday, Kimmel said he had interviewed many political candidates over the years, including Trump himself while he was running for his first term.

"Now that he's president, his FCC has threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network, ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple, traditional editorial decisions, guest bookings it would seem they don't like," Kimmel said.

He added that, in consideration for the network's local stations, particularly ABC affiliates in Texas, his interview with Talarico would not air on television on Thursday and would be posted on YouTube instead.

In a statement to the BBC, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said: "Jimmy Kimmel is play-acting - as he often does - to create a false narrative about this administration's policies."

"[FCC] Chairman [Brendan] Carr has not threatened him regarding interviewing James Talarico, or any other candidate," Ingle added.

The FCC issues broadcast licenses, as well as regulating radio, TV and satellite airwaves.

ABC, which broadcasts Jimmy Kimmel Live!, has been in a feud with the regulator and Carr, a Trump appointee, for months.

In September, Kimmel was temporarily pulled off air for comments he made regarding the shooting of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. That decision was made hours after Carr, a Trump appointee, threatened to act against the ABC and its parent company Disney.

Then in April, Trump and First Lady Melania Trump urged ABC to reprimand Kimmel for a joke he made about her.

Shortly afterwards, the FCC ordered an early review of Disney's television broadcast licences. In response, the ABC last month sued the FCC, arguing it was being unfairly targeted over its editorial content.

Trump has at times said he is considering pulling the FCC licence for several US networks that he said have aired views critical of his presidency.

In February, fellow US late-night host Stephen Colbert accused his network, CBS, of refusing to broadcast his interview with Talarico over fears of retaliation by the FCC. CBS denied it had banned the interview from being aired, saying it only gave "legal guidance".

articles.title: Undercover video exposes Dem Senate nominee's plan to embrace socialists: 'Got to be together'
articles.summary: Roy Cooper's North Carolina Senate race heats up as the former governor rejects calls to repudiate Democratic Socialists of America's influence.
articles.body: Roy Cooper, former North Carolina governor and a Democratic candidate for the Senate, believes his party should incorporate a big-tent approach to an emerging wave of socialist candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). When asked if he would sign the Promise to America, a repudiation of socialist stances put out by moderate Democrats, Cooper said he wouldn’t. "I don’t see any need to," Cooper said in video footage obtained by Fox News Digital. "I think the party needs a wide spectrum, particularly at a time when the Republican Party is shrinking and having all kinds of loyalty tests. I think we need to have all kinds of folks to be a part of our party." FLORIDA BOARD VOTES TO BAN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS FROM PUBLIC COLLEGE ADMISSIONS Cooper’s comment comes as he wages a bid to fill the seat of retiring Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., and win over a historically Republican-leaning state. It also raises questions of whether moderate Democrats believe their platforms can coexist with the aims of the DSA. The DSA espouses positions like abolishing the U.S. Senate, establishing public ownership of corporations and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), according to their website. articles.title: Federal appeals court compares Trump migrant detention policy to Japanese American internment
articles.summary: The 4th Circuit rejected Trump's mass detention policy, comparing it to Japanese Americans' World War II internment, setting the stage for a Supreme Court showdown.
articles.body: A Trump administration policy to detain migrants without a chance for release on bond harkens back to the mass detention of Japanese Americans during World War II, a federal court said Thursday. In a 2-1 decision, the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the administration's mass detention policy, a major part of President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda. "Mass detention of marginalized individuals without due process harkens back to some of the darkest moments in our country’s history," the court wrote. BIDEN JUDGE OVERRULED ON KEY TRUMP IMMIGRATION POLICY Nine federal appeals courts have now separately ruled that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's (ICE) new mandatory detention policy is illegal, concluding it could apply to recent arrivals at or near the border, but not to migrants determined to be living elsewhere within the country. Two other appeals courts have upheld it, meaning the U.S. Supreme Court is likely to take up the case in its upcoming term. TRUMP SCORES SCOTUS ASYLUM WIN — BUT LIBERAL JUSTICE WARNS IT COULD BACKFIRE AT BORDER Immigrant rights groups say basic due process is being violated when longtime residents are denied bond hearings during removal proceedings. "The courts have resoundingly rejected the administration’s cruel policy and its blatant disrespect for the rule of law," said My Khanh Ngo, senior staff attorney with the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. "We are thrilled for our clients and their families." Mass arrests of suspected illegal immigrants during President Donald Trump's second term have prompted widespread protests, particularly in Democratic-led cities like Chicago. In July 2025, the administration announced that it would detain every migrant found anywhere in the U.S. whom ICE determines was not granted permission to enter. A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said the agency was disappointed with Thursday's decision, but said it recently sought a Supreme Court review of a similar decision from the Sixth Circuit. FEDERAL JUDGE IN NEW YORK TIES TRUMP ADMIN HANDS ON ARRESTS AT IMMIGRATION COURTS "Opinions from the Board of Immigration Appeals and two other federal courts of appeals reflect the soundness of DHS’s legal position," the spokesperson said. "This legal position was the nail in the coffin for Biden’s catch and release policies. That is why the left and their activist proxies on the judiciary are resisting it so vigorously. "President Trump and Secretary Mullin are now enforcing the law as it was actually written to keep America safe," the spokesperson added. "As our record in the U.S. Supreme Court demonstrates, the law is on our side." Writing for the majority, 4th Circuit Judge Nicole Berner invoked the mass internment of Japanese Americans during World War II as a warning against sweeping executive detention authority without due process. "The stain of these detentions on our nation—and the judiciary’s abdication of its obligation to protect basic freedoms—continues to haunt us," Berner wrote. articles.title: Deputado e senador: quantos serão eleitos em 2026 e votos necessários? | G1
articles.standfirst: O número de vagas varia conforme o cargo e, no caso dos deputados, a eleição também depende do desempenho dos partidos e das federações.
articles.summary: Número de vagas varia conforme o cargo e, no caso dos deputados, o resultado também depende do desempenho dos partidos e federações.
articles.body:
Imagem urna eletrônica — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

As eleições de 2026 vão definir novos representantes para a Câmara dos Deputados, as Assembleias Legislativas e o Senado Federal. Mas uma dúvida comum entre os eleitores é: quantos parlamentares serão eleitos e quantos votos são necessários para conquistar uma vaga?

A resposta depende do cargo. Deputados federais e estaduais são escolhidos pelo sistema proporcional, enquanto os senadores são eleitos pelo sistema majoritário.

Quantos deputados federais serão eleitos em 2026?

Serão eleitos 513 deputados federais em 2026. As vagas são distribuídas entre os estados e o Distrito Federal conforme a representação definida pela legislação eleitoral.

Os deputados federais têm mandato de quatro anos e são escolhidos pelo sistema proporcional.

Quantos deputados estaduais serão eleitos em 2026?

Serão preenchidas 1.035 vagas de deputado estadual nas Assembleias Legislativas dos estados. No Distrito Federal, serão eleitos ainda 24 deputados distritais, totalizando 1.059 cadeiras estaduais e distritais.

Assim como os deputados federais, deputados estaduais e distritais são eleitos pelo sistema proporcional.

Quantos senadores serão eleitos em 2026?

Em 2026, serão eleitos 54 senadores , dois por estado. O Senado possui 81 cadeiras, e a eleição deste ano vai renovar dois terços da Casa.

O senador tem mandato de oito anos e é eleito pelo sistema majoritário.

Quantos votos são necessários para eleger um deputado?

Não existe um número fixo de votos que garanta a eleição de um deputado federal ou estadual.

Isso acontece porque essas eleições seguem o sistema proporcional. Primeiro, é calculado o quociente eleitoral, que corresponde à divisão dos votos válidos pelo número de vagas em disputa na respectiva eleição.

Depois, os votos recebidos pelos partidos e federações são usados para definir quantas cadeiras cada legenda poderá ocupar. Os candidatos mais votados dentro de cada partido ou federação ocupam essas vagas, respeitadas as regras de votação mínima previstas para a distribuição das cadeiras.

Por isso, o número de votos necessário varia de acordo com o estado, o cargo, a quantidade de votos válidos e o desempenho dos partidos e federações.

Existe votação mínima para um candidato a deputado?

Pelas regras eleitorais, para ocupar uma vaga distribuída pelo quociente partidário, o candidato precisa ter recebido pelo menos 10% do quociente eleitoral.

Nas vagas distribuídas pelas sobras, há duas etapas. Na primeira, participam os partidos e federações que tenham alcançado pelo menos 80% do quociente eleitoral e possuam candidato com votação equivalente a pelo menos 20% desse quociente.

Se ainda restarem cadeiras, elas são distribuídas entre todos os partidos e federações que participaram da eleição, sem exigência de votação mínima para o candidato.

Por isso, não é correto dizer que um candidato precisa simplesmente atingir determinado número de votos para ser eleito deputado.

Quantos votos são necessários para eleger um senador?

A eleição é majoritária. Em 2026, cada estado terá duas vagas em disputa, e serão eleitos os dois candidatos mais votados em cada unidade da Federação.

Dessa forma, também não há uma quantidade mínima de votos previamente definida. O candidato precisa ter mais votos que os concorrentes para ficar entre os dois primeiros colocados no estado.

articles.title: VÍDEO: veja como votar nas duas vagas para o Senado e evite erros | G1
articles.standfirst: Em 2026, eleitor terá dois votos para o Senado e deverá escolher candidatos diferentes. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.summary: Em 2026, eleitor terá dois votos para o Senado e deverá escolher candidatos diferentes. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.body:
Nas eleições de 2026, cada eleitor terá que votar duas vezes para o Senado. Isso acontece porque, neste ano, serão escolhidos dois senadores por estado e pelo Distrito Federal, em uma renovação de dois terços das 81 cadeiras da Casa. Os dois candidatos mais votados em cada unidade da Federação serão eleitos.

Na urna eletrônica, a votação para senador aparecerá em dois momentos diferentes. Primeiro, o eleitor deverá escolher um candidato, digitar o número, conferir o nome e a foto que aparecem na tela e confirmar.

Depois, a urna apresentará uma segunda tela para o voto de senador. Nesse momento, é preciso escolher outro candidato (saiba mais abaixo) .

📍 Em uma série de 50 vídeos, o g1 vai explicar os principais temas das eleições de 2026. Os conteúdos mostram como funcionam as pesquisas, explicam o papel dos cargos em disputa e o funcionamento do Congresso, e trazem orientações práticas para votar. A série também aborda o impacto das novas tecnologias na campanha, como inteligência artificial, deepfakes e influenciadores.

Posso votar duas vezes no mesmo candidato?

Não. Os dois votos para senador precisam ser destinados a candidatos diferentes.

Se o eleitor repetir o número do mesmo candidato nas duas oportunidades, apenas o primeiro voto será considerado válido. O segundo será anulado. Essa regra está prevista na regulamentação do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) para as eleições de 2026.

Por isso, é importante conferir o nome e a foto do candidato antes de confirmar cada voto.

Posso votar em candidato de outro estado?

Não. O eleitor só pode votar nos candidatos que disputam as vagas do estado ou do Distrito Federal onde tem domicílio eleitoral.

Se for digitado o número de um candidato registrado em outra unidade da Federação, o voto não será computado.

Não. Diferentemente das eleições proporcionais, não existe voto de legenda para o Senado.

Para votar em senador, o eleitor precisa escolher um candidato e digitar o número correspondente a ele. Se digitar apenas o número do partido, o voto será considerado nulo.

Na eleição de 2018, a última em que duas vagas para senador estavam em disputa, cerca de 63 milhões de votos para o Senado foram registrados como brancos, nulos ou em apenas uma das vagas — situação que ficou conhecida como "voto incompleto". Os dados, porém, não permitem saber quantos desses casos foram uma escolha deliberada dos eleitores e quantos ocorreram por erro durante a votação.

Veja, passo a passo, como votar para senador

Primeiro voto: digite o número do candidato a senador, confira o nome e a foto e confirme.

Segundo voto: escolha outro candidato, digite o número, confira novamente os dados e confirme.

Não repita o candidato: se o mesmo número for digitado nas duas oportunidades, o segundo voto será nulo.

Vote em candidatos do seu estado: candidatos de outras unidades da Federação não podem receber seu voto.

Não vote apenas na legenda: para senador, o voto é necessariamente em um candidato.

O eleitor também pode optar por não escolher um candidato na segunda oportunidade. Nesse caso, o primeiro voto continua válido, e o segundo pode ser deixado em branco ou ser nulo.

articles.title: STF retoma julgamento sobre mudanças na Lei da Ficha Limpa; resultado pode afetar candidaturas suspensas | G1
articles.standfirst: Se o tribunal validar mudança aprovada pelo Congresso, candidaturas de Garotinho e Arruda podem ser liberadas. Expectativa é de que ministro abra divergência da relatora.
articles.summary: Se o tribunal validar mudança aprovada pelo Congresso, candidaturas de Garotinho e Arruda podem ser liberadas. Expectativa é de que ministro abra divergência da relatora.
articles.body:
O Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) retoma nesta sexta-feira (11) o julgamento que discute mudanças aprovadas pelo Congresso na Lei da Ficha Limpa. O resultado pode impactar campanhas de candidatos que estão sendo questionadas na Justiça Eleitoral.

O julgamento será retomado com o voto do ministro Gilmar Mendes, que pediu mais tempo para analisar o caso em maio.

O julgamento será retomado com o voto do ministro Gilmar Mendes — Foto: Antonio Augusto/STF

Um dos trechos em debate reduz o prazo em que candidatos condenados ficam proibidos de se candidatar, a chamada inelegibilidade. Na prática, a norma reduziu o tempo de punição a políticos cassados.

No STF, há expectativa de que o ministro Gilmar Mendes apresente uma divergência em relação ao entendimento da relatora e abra uma nova corrente votando pela validade de ao menos parte das modificações, como a contagem do prazo para inelegibilidade. Gilmar é crítico à Lei da Ficha Limpa.

🔎 Ainda faltam oito votos, que podem ser inseridos no sistema eletrônico do Supremo até o dia 18. Não há impedimento para que ocorra outro pedido de vista, caso algum ministro entenda que precisa de mais prazo para analisar a ação.

Os ministros analisam uma ação da Rede contra dispositivos da lei, como os marcos utilizados para a contagem do período de oito anos de impedimento para participar da disputa eleitoral.

No voto, a ministra Cármen Lúcia defendeu que as modificações feitas pelo Congresso e sancionadas pelo Executivo esvaziam a legislação , representam um retrocesso e ameaçam o instituto da inelegibilidade. A relatora defendeu o restabelecimento de regras previstas na legislação anterior.

A relatora do caso, ministra Cármen Lúcia — Foto: Luiz Silveira/STF

Cármen Lúcia disse que o STF atua para afastar atos que impeçam, dificultem ou embasam a probidade administrativa e a moralidade pública inerentes ao regime republicano.

"As alterações levadas a efeito pela Lei Complementar n. 219/2025, relacionam-se aos termos inciais e à contagem de prazo para fins de inelegibilidade e estabelecem cenário de patente retrocesso ao que se tinha estabelecido como instrumento de garantia dos princípios republicano, da probidade administrativa e da moralidade pública", avaliou a ministra.

Contagem do prazo para parlamentares cassados por quebra de decoro ou violação das regras constitucionais

Como era na Lei da Ficha Limpa: inelegibilidade pelo prazo restante do mandato perdido mais 8 anos;

Como ficou a partir da lei de 2025: inelegibilidade por 8 anos contados a partir da decisão que decretou a perda do mandato.

Contagem do prazo para governador, vice-governador, prefeito e vice-prefeito que perderem o mandato por descumprirem regras estaduais ou municipais

Como era na Lei da Ficha Limpa: inelegibilidade pelo prazo restante do mandato perdido e mais 8 anos seguintes ao término do mandato para o qual foram eleitos;

Como ficou a partir da lei de 2025: inelegibilidade pelos 8 anos seguintes à decisão que decretou a perda do mandato eletivo.

Contagem do prazo para pessoas condenadas pela Justiça, sem possibilidade de recurso ou por decisão colegiada

Como era na Lei da Ficha Limpa: prazo de inelegibilidade, para todos os crimes previstos na lei, era contado desde a condenação por órgão colegiado até o transcurso do prazo de 8 anos após o cumprimento da pena;

Como ficou a partir da lei da 2025: a regra geral estipulada foi a da inelegibilidade contada a partir da condenação até o prazo de 8 anos. No caso de crimes contra a administração pública, de lavagem de dinheiro, tráfico de drogas, racismo, terrorismo, tortura, crimes contra a vida e a dignidade sexual, hediondos, organização criminosa e redução à condição análoga à de escravo, a inelegibilidade ocorre desde a condenação por órgão colegiado da justiça até o transcurso do prazo de 8 anos após o cumprimento da pena.

Como fica a contagem do prazo para quem renuncia ao mandato para evitar a perda do cargo

Como era na Lei da Ficha Limpa: presidentes, governadores, prefeitos e membros do Legislativo ficavam inelegíveis durante o período restante do mandato para o qual foram eleitos e nos 8 anos seguinte;

Como ficou a partir da lei de 2025: presidentes, governadores, prefeitos e membros do Legislativo ficam inelegíveis nos 8 anos seguintes à renúncia ao cargo.

Prazo limite no caso de inelegibilidade por improbidade administrativa acumulada com outra condenação posterior

Como era na Lei da Ficha Limpa: não havia esse prazo limite;

Como ficou a partir da lei de 2025: prazo máximo de 12 anos se durante o prazo de inelegibilidade por improbidade houver outra condenação que afete a capacidade eleitoral.

articles.title: Trump says he would ‘probably’ be able to make deals with Democrats
articles.summary: President Trump said he would “probably” be able to make deals with Democrats should they take back majorities in Congress — but warned he would also work to block their agenda. “I’ll be a block. I’ll end up being a blocker. I’ll block all of their bad stuff for two years,” Trump said in an…
articles.body:
President Trump said he would “probably” be able to make deals with Democrats should they take back majorities in Congress — but warned he would also work to block their agenda.

“I’ll be a block. I’ll end up being a blocker. I’ll block all of their bad stuff for two years,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News’s Laura Ingraham on “The Ingraham Angle.”

“It won’t be the same , but I’ll be a blocker. What can I tell you? And probably be able to make deals with them,” he continued.

When asked by Ingraham if he will campaign harder than he ever has before November’s midterms, Trump said no.

“The hardest I ever campaigned [was] because I had to win,” the president said. “I took four months, no empty days, no empty hours. I made speeches all day.”

When asked if the upcoming midterms were just as important as his presidential bid because of their potential impact on his legacy, Trump said, “It’s never as important.”

“I’m campaigning for other people,” he said.

The interview comes as Trump is galvanizing Republicans in Dallas, Texas, for the party’s midterm convention.

Trump told reporters last week that he will spend the final 30 days before November’s midterm elections campaigning for candidates in 35 competitive races. The president also said he would travel to Alaska to campaign for incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R), who is facing an uphill reelection bid.

articles.title: WATCH: Socialist protester blames 'provocateurs' after assaults at 'closest entry point' to Trump convention
articles.summary: A socialist protester blamed right-wing provocateurs after Dallas police in riot gear arrested two near the Republican National Committee convention.
articles.body: A socialist "Never Trumpers" protester blamed "conservative provocateurs" for a tense confrontation with police that resulted in multiple arrests just outside the Republican National Committee's midterm convention in Dallas. Videos posted on social media Thursday afternoon showed what appeared to be hundreds of Never Trumpers confronting Dallas police just blocks from where the president was set to deliver his convention-closing speech. Authorities responded with a strong show of force that included officers in apparent riot gear. The Dallas Police Department confirmed with Fox News Digital that two protesters were arrested on charges related to their actions during the protest. The department said that officers assigned to the area arrested the two protesters after it said they "assaulted a counter-protester" and "obstructed a road." The department said the suspects’ names and specific charges will be released after they are booked into jail. CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN? GOP BETS ON TRUMP AT HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION Fox News Digital spoke with a protester named Rick Majumdar, who was wearing a shirt with the initials for the Freedom Road Socialist Organization (FRSO), which, according to its website, is a "national organization of revolutionaries fighting for socialism in the United States." Majumdar said that the protest was organized by the Dallas Against the Trump Agenda Coalition, which, he said, consists of 16 "faith-based organizations, pro-immigrants’ rights groups and labor organizations." "We're here to protest the Republican agenda, the Trump agenda and all its policies that it has enacted over the last few years," he explained. "The march is an important event, we feel, against this convention that's happening for the last two days." REPUBLICANS HEAD TO DALLAS WITH ONE MISSION: DEFY HISTORY AND WIN BIG He said that, during the group's march, "we encountered some street closures by the police" and that officers arrested a couple of protesters who "were at the front of the group." Pressed on why the protesters were arrested, Majumdar said, "Those people were trying to draw people away from rioting provocateurs, and I think the police heard something. And they immediately tackled two of them and arrested them, and some of them even pulled out their guns as well." The protest came amid heightened concerns over political violence and the targeting of public figures. It also coincided with the first anniversary of the assassination of conservative activist and Turning Point USA co-founder Charlie Kirk. CHARLIE KIRK CONTINUES TO INSPIRE REPUBLICANS AS PARTY RALLIES FOR MIDTERM BATTLE: 'HAVE COURAGE' SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Majumdar did not answer whether the protesters blocked any roads but said the confrontation occurred at the "closest entry point" to the convention. articles.title: Top Trump official reveals how 30-minute military op unlocked Venezuela oil windfall for US buyers
articles.summary: Energy Secretary Chris Wright says the Trump administration is tapping Venezuela's 300 billion barrels of oil reserves to expand supply and cut prices.
articles.body: DALLAS, Texas — The 30-minute U.S. military operation that removed Nicolás Maduro from power has helped clear the way for a sweeping expansion of Venezuela’s battered energy sector, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said, sharing that the country’s national energy production will more than double by the end of 2027. "Chevron is going to more than double their energy production. In fact, that national energy production in Venezuela will more than double by the end of next year from the intervention on Jan. 3 this year," Wright told Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the RNC Midterm Convention. Wright said the military actions in Venezuela helped open the door for a major increase in oil production as the administration has increasingly taken an active role in the socialist country as part of a broader push to expand U.S. influence and investment. U.S. forces entered Venezuela for Operation Absolute Resolve Jan. 3, capturing Maduro and his wife Flores. War Secretary Pete Hegseth said the attack was part of "massive joint military and law enforcement raid" and lasted less than 30 minutes. TRUMP TOUTS ACCESS TO 65 BILLION BARRELS OF VENEZUELAN OIL IN DEAL HE SAYS WILL SLASH GAS PRICES "You had 25 years of communist dictatorship. The standard of living has just plummeted in Venezuela. Eight million Venezuelans fled. About a million of them, and not all of them good actors, came to the United States of America. People tried to beg, borrow, bribe, anything they could to change the Venezuelan government. No luck," Wright said. "President Trump is an out-of-the-box, bold foreign policy leader. "A brief military operation, arrest two criminals and now we have leverage over the government. It’s an existing government. Are they perfect? No. But we have a lot of leverage." Chevron scored an investment of more than $7 billion over five years and more than double its Venezuelan oil production to 600,000 barrels per day, according to its press release. Venezuela controls more than 300 billion barrels of crude reserves, roughly 20% of the world’s total. Despite holding an estimated 17% of the world’s oil reserves, Venezuela produces only about 1% of global output after years of political instability and deteriorating infrastructure undermined its energy industry. TOP ENERGY TRADER HAILS TRUMP'S VENEZUELA OIL DEAL AS A 'GENERATIONAL WIN' FOR GAS PRICES Wright said shifting the center of global energy production toward the Western Hemisphere will put the U.S. at the center and major producers, including Canada, Guyana and Mexico supplying more of the world’s oil and gas. Millions of barrels of new Venezuelan production would be processed through U.S. refineries and produced using American rigs and infrastructure, creating thousands of American jobs, according to the White House. STATE DEPARTMENT ANNOUNCES 'TOTAL COMPLIANCE' FROM VENEZUELAN GOVERNMENT IN RELIEF EFFORTS AFTER MADURO ARREST The administration’s emerging approach to Venezuela could use U.S. leverage with energy investment to prompt political change. That deal comes with added importance as the war with Iran disrupts oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. The average U.S. price for regular gasoline rose to about $4.22 a gallon Wednesday, according to AAA, up from roughly $3.19 a year earlier. This is a nation sounding death to America and doing everything they can to implement it. But we've massively grown United States natural gas exports, good for our economy, good for the world economy," Wright said.

articles.title: Vance declares Democrats ‘party of hatred,’ says party has moved beyond big government, censorship
articles.summary: Vice President JD Vance will use a deeply personal speech to reflect on the legacy of late friend Charlie Kirk, the joys of fatherhood and the future he hopes America can provide.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Vice President JD Vance argued Thursday that Democrats have moved so far to the left that they no longer resemble the party of past Democratic presidents, branding the modern Democratic Party the "party of hatred" in a fiery convention address first obtained by Fox News Digital. "They're not the party of FDR or JFK. Hell, they're not even the party of Bill Clinton anymore," Vance said. "The Democrats are the party of hatred. They're the party that despises America and the people who built it." Vance used the closing night of the Republican convention to build that charge across a series of cultural and economic flashpoints, pointing to a Democratic candidate's attack on the nuclear family, his own clash with Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and what he cast as a broader Democratic message telling American children "who they ought to hate." TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE The vice president contrasted that portrait with what he called Americans' "birthright" — the opportunity to build a family, own a home, find meaningful work and pass a better country to their children — while honoring his late friend Charlie Kirk one year after his assassination. On the anniversary of Turning Point USA's co-founder Charlie Kirk’s death, Vance honored his friend. "I was elected Vice President of the United States one year ago today, on September the 10th of last year, that good friend was taken from us when Charlie was assassinated. Now, Charlie left behind two children, two little kids. They were too young to fully understand," said Vance. Vance recalled Kirk’s message to young men that few callings are greater than falling in love, starting a family and becoming a father — words that have taken on new meaning for the vice president since he and Second Lady Usha Vance welcomed their son Alec in July. He used Kirk's legacy to transition into touting what he called Americans' "birthright" exceptionalism. "I believe the Founders built this nation on a promise that echoes our Creator: That every American child is born an heir, born with a birthright," said Vance. "Born with the right to inherit the blessings of this country. Not because of who their parents are. Not because of what they look like or where they come from. But because they are Americans." Vance used the opportunity to outline his vision for rebuilding the nuclear family, while taking shots at Democrats. "I think about what the Democrats have said about our shared birthright as Americans, or frankly, the lack thereof in Michigan. One Democrat in particular, one candidate has said, and I quote ‘f the nuclear family.’ What are you even talking about?" said Vance. "They come not from a desire to serve you or our fellow Americans, but they come from a very deep emptiness in the soul," he added. CROWD ERUPTS AS VANCE SMACKS DOWN PROTESTER WAVING MEXICAN FLAG: ‘GET YOUR A-- OVER THERE’ A protester emerged carrying Mexican and Palestinian flags, prompting Vance to respond, "What the people at home missed is that we just had a protestor interrupting us and waving the Mexican flag." "Well. Well, my friend, if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I'll buy you the plane ticket," the vice president said. Vance said the protester should have been waving the American flag, adding that it is a symbol of the fight for the American dream. "This fall, the Democrats are running candidates who will tell your children what they're allowed to say, how they're allowed to live, and importantly, who they ought to hate. Because that's what the Democrat Party is about in 2026. It's not about you, it's about foreign fraudsters, and it's about who they hate," said Vance. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Vance spoke about the economy former President Joe Biden left, pointing to housing costs and Americans competing against illegal immigrants in the job market. "Our nation became a place where you had to be rich to enjoy what used to be the birthright of every ordinary middle-class life," he said. Vance touted his wins from leading the White House Task Force on fraud and calling out Democrats for "refus[ing] to prosecute the crime." He said the task force has found $250 billion of fraud just since he was appointed fraud czar. Vance took aim at Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, with whom he has sparred in recent weeks after El-Sayed made comments about the second family. "He saw me describing what a decent man and my papa was genuinely a decent and good man. He saw me talking about my papa and his work and his history and what he loved and what he cared about. And you know what old Abdul did? He asked mockingly whether I'd be willing to bring Usha back in time to meet Papa," Vance resurfaced. Vance said El-Sayed saw "the color of his skin, sees his background, and decides that he could never have loved my wife." "Abdul himself was raised by his own white step-grandparents. He knows exactly that kind of bond and what it looks like in a family, and he chose any way to say that a man like my grandfather couldn't have love from the bottom of his heart," Vance added.

articles.title: Is Trump's $5,000 pledge a sign of panic?
articles.summary: Even by Trump's own unconventional standards, his promise to voters was bizarre, writes North America editor Sarah Smith.
articles.body:
We all know that Donald Trump does not feel the need to adhere to the normal rules of political campaigning. Even by his own unconventional standards, his extravagant promise to pay every American citizen $5,000 (£3,700) if the Republicans win the midterm elections was bizarre.

This enormous cash pledge was not the headline of his keynote address at the first night of his midterms Republican convention on Wednesday.

He slipped in the mention about an hour into his lengthy speech - just when the audience's attention was starting to waver.

The president offered no details on how this more than one-trillion-dollar pledge will be paid for or how the payments would be distributed.

Asked for more information, the White House said in a statement that "the announcement is the latest proof that President Trump does what the so-called 'experts' say cannot be done: he delivers for the American people", but gave no more specifics about how it would be implemented.

The announcement itself was met with enthusiastic applause from supporters inside the Republican convention arena in Dallas, Texas.

But Republicans in tight races in November's election - who need to win over sceptical swing voters, including moderate Republicans and independents - largely stayed away from the event.

And many of Trump's fellow Republicans were clearly taken by surprise. Some welcomed the announcement, but Republicans that are more critical of Trump were quick to denounce it.

Trump says every adult American will get $5,000 if Republicans win midterms

Conservatives who have clashed with Trump before, especially over how the federal debt has continued to balloon under his presidency, were scathing in their response.

Thomas Massie, the Republican representative from Kentucky who lost his primary over Trump criticisms earlier this year, posted on X: "I don't know about you all, but frankly I'm insulted by the notion that my vote this November could be bought for 5k. Not to mention the inflation this would cause. All things considered, I cannot in good conscience accept a penny less than 10k!"

Senator Susan Collins, who swerved Dallas to campaign in Maine where she's facing a tight race for re-election, said: "Tax and spending decisions should be made based on the needs of the American people and the state of the economy, they should not appear to be tied to election results."

Democrats for their part have labelled it an "empty promise".

Legal experts say it's unlikely Trump could approve such a vast sum via a presidential executive order - but the president suggested on Thursday he wouldn't be going to Congress.

Speaking to the BBC's US partner CBS, he said he didn't think Congress would need to approve the spending, before adding: "I think they will do it, if we needed it."

But plenty of fiscally conservative Republican representatives would likely refuse to support this kind of spending.

Former Republican Representative Bob Good dismissed the "Trump dividend" as a "socialist vote-buying scheme".

But this convention was a reminder that Trump still dominates the party and, in the House of Representative at least, he has previously made them bend to his will on policies that don't chime with traditional conservative positions.

This is not the first time President Trump has made a cash promise to voters. Americans are still waiting for the $2,000 cheques he said they would each receive from the revenue generated from his trade tariffs. And the $5,000 payments that Elon Musk proposed would come from his Doge spending cuts have never materialised.

Trump has delivered on his promise to set up Trump saving accounts with a government contribution of $1,000 for children born during his term in office. And all members of the US military got a payment of $1,776 to celebrate America's 250th anniversary.

Is it a sign that Donald Trump fears that he is on course for a major defeat in November that he feels the need to make this kind of eye-catching election promise?

Despite the president not featuring on the ballot, voters often treat midterm elections as a referendum on the sitting president - and often the party in power struggles.

And less than two months out from election day, Trump faces historically low approval ratings.

His war with Iran has become increasingly unpopular, and its knock-on effects are hitting Americans at the petrol pump. Affordability is still a top issue for voters, and while inflation is down from its post-Covid peak under Joe Biden, it remains stubbornly high.

So does this pledge suggest an element of panic that he pulled this policy out of his back pocket before many of his closest allies had been told about it?

It is undoubtedly a highly unorthodox way of launching a major election pledge.

But Trump's political success has been built on his norm-breaking way of doing business.

His latest ploy could work – but only if voters believe he is serious about writing them a cheque.

Can Trump really pay $5,000 to every American adult?

Four key takeaways from Republican midterms convention

articles.title: Top GOP senator reveals what Dem colleagues are fretting about behind closed doors
articles.summary: Senate Republican John Barrasso says Democratic senators privately admit the progressive wave led by Abdul El-Sayed and others is their future.
articles.body: DALLAS — As Republicans huddle for a last show of unity before the home stretch of the midterm elections, a top Senate Republican revealed what his Democratic colleagues are predicting about the future of their party. Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., told Fox News Digital that in private, his colleagues across the aisle are wringing their hands over the insurgent progressive wave that has fast become the standard-bearer of the Democratic Party during this election cycle. "It's surprising how the energy of the Democrat Party has moved to the far, far left," Barrasso said during an interview at the Republican National Committee midterm convention. TOP REPUBLICAN NAMES WHO HE SAYS IS REALLY LEADING DEMOCRATS — AND IT'S NOT SCHUMER OR JEFFRIES "Those are the people that are driving the party. And the concern that I have, talking to other colleagues in the Senate, who they’ll say that is the future of their party," he continued. Republicans are trying to fight against history and anxious voters feeling the crunch on their wallets, and as the war in Iran continues to sputter on without a clear end in sight. The convention in Dallas is meant to hammer home that while President Donald Trump’s name isn’t on the ballot, his agenda, and the incumbents and fresh candidates that could execute it, are. TRUMP'S $5,000 DIVIDEND CHECKS WOULD COME WITH A MAJOR CATCH UNDER GOP SENATOR'S PLAN While that push to energize Trump’s base to hit the polls in November ensues, key races across the Senate map have seen progressive and far-left candidates emerge as the standard-bearers for the party during this cycle. REPUBLICAN SOUNDS ALARM ON RISING DEM STAR: 'THIS GUY’S GOING TO BE A PROBLEM' El-Sayed and Talarico, in particular, have been targeted heavily during the convention, which Trump declared was, in part, dedicated to ensuring Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton would win out and prevent the Lone Star State from turning a shade of purple. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
