articles.title: Vance positions himself as a fighter for family values and a ‘national birthright’
articles.summary: The vice president drew on the birth of his fourth child and the one-year anniversary of Charlie Kirk’s death in his GOP midterm convention speech.
articles.body: DALLAS — Vice President JD Vance on Thursday offered his young family — in particular, his newborn son — as a model and a window to the future that the potential 2028 presidential contender envisions for America. In a speech here at the Republicans’ midterm convention, Vance broadly criticized Democrats who he said do not share his values. He also homed in specifically on two Democratic candidates this fall in Michigan: Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed and Will Lawrence, who is seeking a House seat. Vance seized on Lawrence’s since-deleted social media posts that were critical of the nuclear family. “I’ve thought a lot, ladies and gentlemen, about what is the birthright of this newest of Americans, my little boy,” Vance told the crowd at American Airlines Center. “And I think about what the Democrats have said about our shared birthright as Americans or, frankly, the lack thereof.” He added a moment later, “To the radicals who wish to abolish my family and the thousands and millions of other families all across our country, we have a simple message for them: Stay the hell away from our kids!” Vance’s speech on the convention’s closing night represented something of an unofficial passing of the torch from the term-limited Trump to his 42-year-old vice president, who is seen as a leading candidate for president in two years. At one point, the audience broke out with chants of “48! 48!” Vance would be the 48th president if he succeeds Trump. “We’ve got to take care of business this November,” Vance replied, sticking to his common refrain when he is confronted with speculation about his White House ambitions. “Then we’ll worry about what comes next.” Later, in a moment that captured the unique dynamic of playing understudy to a president who relishes being the center of attention, Vance passed the torch back. Trump, who spoke for an hour and 45 minutes the night before, returned to the stage for closing remarks that lasted about 25 minutes. While Trump’s words Wednesday and Thursday effectively made the midterms a referendum on his time in office, Vance offered a more forward-looking case that at times scanned as his case for what should come next. “I can’t help but think about what it is that we’re fighting for and what it is that we want for all of our children,” Vance said. “What I want for my family, I want for your family, too.” He added: “This country was handed down to us by our parents and their parents before them. We received this national birthright, and we are going to fight for it by electing Republicans this November.” A person close to Vance told NBC News that he will begin giving a White House bid more serious thought after the November elections and is not necessarily expected to reach or announce an immediate decision. Republicans routinely mention Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as Trump’s two likeliest successors. Rubio, who ran for president in 2016, has said he does not plan to run and has signaled that Vance will have his support if he does. Another potential 2028 contender, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, spoke during Thursday’s convention program. He focused his remarks tightly on 2026 races, leveling criticism at Democratic Senate candidates such as El-Sayed and Texas state Rep. James Talarico. “As one Democrat president put it long ago, before his party had lost their ever-loving minds, we have a rendezvous with destiny,” Cruz said, invoking Franklin Roosevelt. “Together, we must stand and fight for the Constitution. We must stand and fight for freedom. We must stand and defeat the communists. We must stand and defeat the Islamists.” Cruz, who also ran in 2016, has made several moves over the last year to position himself against Vance. Those moves have not escaped Vance’s notice. When he was asked at a White House briefing last week about Cruz’s prospects, Vance offered a sarcastic reply: “Clearly, Ted is a very authentic and likable guy, and I’m sure he’ll do great.” Vance, like others who spoke Thursday, also used his speech to reflect on his friendship with conservative activist Charlie Kirk on the first anniversary of his assassination. He offered a message to Kirk’s two young children. “I hope that one day they will watch and they will know and they will understand what I’m trying to say to them tonight,” Vance said. “History will record that your father was a great man.” At another point, Vance was briefly interrupted by what he said was a protester waving Mexico’s flag. “Well, my friend,” Vance responded, “if you love Mexico so much, get your ass over there. I’ll buy you the plane ticket.” Vance, known for his conservative populism, also made overtures to more moderate and independent voters. “Look, I’m not asking anybody to agree with me on every single issue. I’m not asking anybody to agree on every single policy of the administration,” he said. “What I am asking you to do is to recognize the contrast with the radicals and recognize the achievements of the last 18 months. We have done a lot, my friends, and we can do a lot more if we fight together.” Vance reserved his vitriol for Democrats and the progressive left. He went on an extended riff against El-Sayed, who last month mockingly wondered whether Vance would take his Indian American wife, Usha Vance, back in time to meet his late grandfather. Vance also alluded to El-Sayed’s alliance with Hasan Piker, a Twitch streamer who previously said on a livestream that “America deserved 9/11.” Piker has since apologized for the remark, which has become a staple of Republican campaigning this year. “This is who the Democrats are now,” Vance said. “They’re the party that can find sympathy for the terrorists who perpetrated 9/11, but they say that people with names like James Vance are incapable of loving people with names like Usha. And they couldn’t be more wrong.” Known previously for a bestselling memoir that chronicled his rough childhood, Vance has been on a fast political rise since he won a Senate seat in Ohio in 2022. Just days after he survived an assassination attempt in 2024, Trump selected him over Rubio and others to be his running mate, opening doors that have helped position Vance as an heir apparent. Vance is the Republican National Committee’s finance chair — an unprecedented move for a sitting vice president that has given him an opportunity to connect with big-money donors who can be helpful to his political career. On Thursday, for example, Vance headlined an RNC fundraiser here that brought in $2 million, two people familiar with the event said. He also headlined a breakfast for conventiongoers from Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Ohio and Hawaii. Another speaker at that event, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, referred to Vance’s backstory and explicitly promoted him as a 2028 candidate. “Every single study would have told you that that kid will probably not make it in life. And what is he today? The vice president of the United States,” said Moreno, whose remarks were heard by NBC News before an organizer told a reporter to leave the event, which was not intended to be open to media. “I think there’s a chance,” Moreno added, “that in two years when we’re together again for a convention that we’ll be nominating him as the next president.” Moreno, who supported Rubio’s 2016 campaign for president, said Vance is his first choice for president and that he, like others, does not believe Rubio would run against him. Moreno, noting the recent birth of Vance’s fourth child, also said he believes he will take his time to make a decision. “I think he’s going to do a lot of soul-searching,” Moreno said. “He does have four little kids. Being president of the United States is not a small job. It is soul-sucking. Running for president is beyond comprehension.” Moreno added, “If he calls me and asks if he should run, I’d say, ‘Hell yes, and how can I help?’” In other conversations around the convention, Vance’s and Rubio’s names topped the lists of many delegates and party leaders when they were asked whom they could see at the top of the 2028 ticket. Others took more of a wait-and-see approach. “You know, I can name, you know, half a dozen people that are great, starting with our vice president, our secretary of state, numerous governors and senators,” said Vince Galko, a former top official at the Pennsylvania Republican Party. “We have a spoil of riches right now and a great bench to pull from.”

articles.body:
Vice President Vance issued sharp criticism of James Talarico in the Democratic Senate candidate’s backyard, while speaking at the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday evening.

Talarico, a state lawmaker, is running against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) this November to replace incumbent GOP Sen. John Cornyn.

“But this Talarico guy, he will not shut up about how there are six genders,” Vance told the crowd. “He will not shut up about how, quote, ‘God is non-binary.’ I don’t know what the hell that even means, my friends.”

Republicans have repeatedly condemned the Democratic nominee’s criticism of Christian nationalism and his decision as a state legislator to oppose a ban on transgender student athletes competing in girls’ sports.

“He won’t shut up about having traditional Christian values makes you a bigot, and I gotta say, a guy that age who is so obsessed and focused on transgender children — I don’t know about you, but I never want to see that guy’s web browser history,” Vance said. “It’s not a good place. We’d rather be here.”

Talarico told Fox News on Wednesday that he supports banning trans athletes from women’s and girls’ sports “if it endangers safety or fairness.”

“Every sport has to be safe and fair,” the Democrat added.

The vice president also issued broad criticism of the Democrats during his speech, accusing the party of moving away from its roots to become “the party of hatred.”

“They’re the party that despises America and the people who built it,” Vance added.

Vance urged GOP voters to turn out to vote in the midterm elections, in which the Republican Party is fighting to maintain its majority in both chambers of Congress.

“I’m asking you, my fellow Republicans, to remember that this November is so much more than red team versus blue team. It’s so much more than having good politicians in Washington,” he said.

“It’s about sending a message to the Democratic Party that if you send your crazies, we’re going to send you packing,” Vance continued. “It’s about fighting for our fellow citizens, for their dreams and for the inheritance of a great nation that all of us are going to leave behind.”

articles.title: Trump leads convention in pledge: ‘You go to h—’ if you don’t vote
articles.summary: President Trump closed out the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday by urging attendees to pledge to go out and vote in November’s midterm elections. “Please raise your right hand,” Trump told a stadium packed with his supporters as he was met with some laughter. “I pledge to the greatest president in the history…
articles.body:
President Trump closed out the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday by urging attendees to pledge to go out and vote in November’s midterm elections.

“Please raise your right hand,” Trump told a stadium packed with his supporters as he was met with some laughter.

“I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States that loves us so much he can’t even breathe, that I will go out with my family, my friends,” he continued.

“I don’t care if I’m registered or not. I’m going to try and cheat like hell like they do. There’s never been bigger cheaters. I don’t care,” he said. “I am going to go out and I am going to get my friends, my family, and we are going to vote on Nov. 3rd or we are going to vote before that.”

Trump said it went without saying that people would vote Republican.

“Okay. So help me God,” he concluded the pledge.

“You know what happens if you don’t vote? You go to hell,” he added. “You know that, okay? You go to hell, and I don’t want that to happen to you. So please go and vote, because together we will defeat the communists.”

The pledge, which some in the crowd tried to repeat, came at the end of a notably succinct speech compared to his remarks Wednesday night, as he seeks to gin up enthusiasm among his conservative base ahead of the midterms.

Republicans are facing historical headwinds in their battle to maintain their majorities in the House and the Senate, given that the president’s party normally loses seats in their first midterm election.

Additionally, Trump is facing declining approval ratings and a growing frustration with the economy, which appears to have impacted Republican candidates on the generic ballot.

Trump and his Republican allies are leaning into a strategy of turning out as much of his base as possible in a bid to defy historical trends and a poor national environment.

On Thursday, Trump reiterated his proposal to give $5,000 to every U.S. adult if Republicans retain their majorities on Capitol Hill — an idea he pitched Wednesday night that met pushback from both sides of the aisle on Thursday.

“If we win the midterms, we will on the other hand, we will provide a, let’s call it a Trump dividend, $5,000 for every adult citizen in our country,” he said. “And we can do that because our country has never done better. We’re taking in trillions, trillions of dollars. There’s never been any country, not even close, that’s come anywhere near.”

“We win $5,000 for every adult. We love our adults,” he added.

articles.title: Iran war largely ignored at the Republican midterm convention
articles.summary: Aside from mentions by Trump and top administration officials, speakers at the convention mostly avoided talking about the war.
articles.body: America has been at war with Iran for more than six months — but it was far from a top issue at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas this week. The war wasn’t entirely absent: Administration officials defended it. President Donald Trump talked about the war in his speeches Wednesday and Thursday nights. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also referred to it in a video shown Wednesday. Vice President JD Vance didn’t explicitly mention Iran in his address Thursday night, but he paid tribute to slain conservative activist Charlie Kirk, saying he “hated war” and acknowledging that there are “people who love what we’ve done and people who don’t” while urging conservatives to stick together in the midterms. Aside from that, essentially none of the other speakers discussed the war, which is a point of major concern for Americans ahead of the midterm elections. The recent NBC News Decision Desk Poll found just 31% of adults approving of Trump’s handling of the war, with 69% disapproving. Robert Jeffress, the senior pastor of First Baptist Church in Dallas, told the crowd Thursday night that “we are in a war” — but he clarified that he was talking about a “cosmic” battle between good and evil, not the war with Iran. The decision by other top Republican officials and candidates fighting for re-election to ignore the war reflected its growing unpopularity and a recognition that it’s not an issue the party is eager to run on in November. Trump was willing to defend it — saying it will end “shortly” after Election Day — but few others outside the administration seemed to want to own it. As Vance alluded to, parts of Trump’s base have been uneasy with the war since the U.S. and Israel launched strikes in late February. Trump, after all, had long positioned himself in opposition to the traditionally hawkish tendencies of the Republican establishment, running on an “America First” platform that eschewed foreign entanglements and “forever wars.” That dissatisfaction has grown. Trump’s approval rating on the war has hardly shifted since the spring, according to the NBC News Decision Desk Poll. But there has been a noticeable change in intensity, particularly among Republicans. The survey found that the share of self-identified Republicans who say they strongly approve of Trump’s handling of the war has dropped 18 percentage points since the spring, now standing at 30%. That’s driven primarily by a 21-point decrease in the share of self-identified MAGA Republicans who say they strongly approve of the war, with 43% of that group strongly approving. Few outright disapprove of Trump’s moves on Iran, but more have shifted to saying they “somewhat” approve. The Trump administration initially signaled that it expected the war to last just four or five weeks. Since then, Trump and his top officials have repeatedly insisted that the war is almost over — or, at times, said it has already been won. Recently, Vance said he didn’t even really consider it a war at all. Since the U.S. attacked Iran, 18 U.S. service members have been killed. Roughly 50,000 troops are deployed across the Middle East. There were few mentions of those troops at the convention, as well, although Jack Graham, the pastor who delivered the opening invocation Wednesday, paid tribute to them: “We pray for our military as they protect our freedom, our faith and our future. Bring our troops home safely and soon.”

articles.title: Oz wants ‘unexpected star’ Fetterman to cross the aisle and become Republican
articles.summary: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid (CMM) Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said on a podcast Thursday that he wants Sen. John Fetterman (D), his rival in Pennsylvania’s 2022 Senate race, to cross the aisle and join the Republican party. Oz’s comments come a day after Fetterman’s surprise video appearance at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention…
articles.body:
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid (CMM) Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz said on a podcast Thursday that he wants Sen. John Fetterman (D), his rival in Pennsylvania’s 2022 Senate race, to cross the aisle and join the Republican party.

Oz’s comments come a day after Fetterman’s surprise video appearance at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas.

“I want everyone in the party. God works in mysterious ways, but they’re brilliant and loving ways and I’m very happy for that,” Oz said on Harry Cole’s podcast , “Harry Cole Saves the West.”

“Would you like to see him come over to Republican?” Cole asked of Fetterman.

“Of course. We as many people as are willing to be brave and push back on an orthodoxy or a rhetoric that doesn’t actually describe reality,” Oz responded.

Oz lost to Fetterman by five points, despite the Democrat suffering a stroke in the middle of the campaign.

Fetterman on Wednesday appeared in a video praising fellow Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick (R) at the midterm convention, which stirred up anger among some Democrats.

“Why am I here talking to you today?” Fetterman said in the video. “Because, well, I’m a commonsense Democrat.”

“David McCormick is the kind of senator that gets the job done,” he added, noting the two senators would work with President Trump to assist Pennsylvania’s manufacturing industry.

Pittsburgh-area Rep. Chris Deluzio (D) said in an interview with CNN’s Jake Tapper that the Democratic senator has been “nowhere to be found” in the state and that “he’s spending his time, frankly, going on right-wing media to bash the Democrats.”

Deluzio told Chris Stirewalt on NewNation’s “The Hill Sunday” that he may challenge Fetterman when his seat is up in 2028.

In addition to Oz’s Republican comments on Fetterman, political commentator Bill O’Reilly said Wednesday that he believes Fetterman is, “going to be a Republican,” pointing at the senator’s relationship with President Trump and McCormick.

articles.title: RNC finale ‘all about Vance’ as GOP base looks to 2028
articles.summary: Vice President Vance roused the closing night crowd at the Republican National Committee’s Dallas convention amid growing chatter about his 2028 prospects. The Thursday night keynote — interrupted at one point with chants of “48” — offered the vice president a chance to charm the base that will be critical if he decides to run…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance roused the closing night crowd at the Republican National Committee’s Dallas convention amid growing chatter about his 2028 prospects.

The Thursday night keynote — interrupted at one point with chants of “48” — offered the vice president a chance to charm the base that will be critical if he decides to run to succeed President Trump in the next election.

“We got to take care of business this November. Then we’ll worry about what comes next,” Vance said in response to the crowd.

Widely seen as the MAGA movement’s heir apparent, Vance has played coy about his future plans as Republicans steer focus to winning the midterms. But attendees were quick to say they have their eye on Vance for 2028, alongside Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was not attending.

“Team Vance right here,” said Kim Simmons, an attendee from Texas, when asked about 2028 after the vice president’s speech.

“All about Vance,” said Texan Martha McCullough.

Debra Shaver and Rosie Swanson, a pair of attendees from Texas, said “Vance-Rubio” in unison when asked about the party’s next presidential ticket.

“Either one of ‘em,” said Dedra Taie of Texas’s Collin County.

“I can’t wait to see Vance. He’s gorgeous,” said Michelle Taylor, an attendee from Houston, ahead of the vice president’s speech.

Rubio, who ran against Trump in 2016, has seen his profile rise as he maneuvers on the international stage. He was abroad during the convention, and told a Columbian news station this week that he has no plans at this point to launch another run for the White House.

“If it’s one or the other, I don’t care which way that ticket goes, as long as they’re both on the ticket,” said Nola Nemeth-Odens, an attendee from Texas, of a Vance-Rubio ticket.

“I’m sure there are other viable candidates, we just don’t know them yet. But those two articulate the message most effectively,” she said.

Others stressed that the convention showcased a wealth of options for the GOP.

“There’s a lot that will happen between now and then, and they’re both extremely talented, so I think we’ve got a deep bench on the Republican side,” said Barb Novak, an attendee from Minnesota.

In an average of polls compiled by Race to the WH, testing a potential 2028 GOP primary, Vance was the clear leader with 40 percent, followed by Rubio at around 22 percent. They were the only two names in double-digit territory, with Donald Trump Jr. notching third place at around 9 percent.

Vance won a 2028 straw poll at the Conservative Political Action Conference earlier this year, followed by Rubio. A similar poll was not expected at the RNC’s first-ever midterm convention.

An Emerson College/The Hill survey released last month showed Rubio outperforming Vance in five match-ups against Democrats, with the exception of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who held a 5-point edge against both Republicans.

The vice president during his speech Thursday sought to draw a contrast between Republicans and Democrats through citing the accomplishments of the Trump administration.

“I’m not asking you to agree with every policy of our administration. I’m asking you to recognize the contrast with the radicals, and the achievements of the last 18 months,” Vance said.

Vance also reflected on his friendship with the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, using his legacy to reach out to voters upset with the administration, noting Kirk “hated war,” including in the Middle East.

“Do what Charlie did: Do not throw the baby out with the bathwater. Don’t give the country over to a bunch of crazy people because you happen to disagree with us on a policy issue here or there,” Vance said.

Some other potential White House contenders, including Trump Jr. and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), also filled out the day-two speakers list.

Cruz painted the Democratic Party as an existential threat, and also knocked Democrat James Talarico, who is easing ahead of Trump-backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) in the latest polling on the race.

Both days of the convention were characterized by a focus on the Lone Star State against the backdrop of a closer-than-expected Senate race.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, and Reps. Monica De La Cruz and Brandon Gill also addressed the conference, along with a trio of Republican candidates for the House and Dallas’s Democrat-turned-Republican mayor.

Paxton addressed the convention crowd on the first night of the Dallas crowd, under U.S. and Lone Star State flags hung from the ceiling facing the stage — and got a double-edged shout-out in both of Trump’s remarks.

Trump doubled down Thursday on his criticism that he doesn’t “like the way Ken dresses,” “talks” or “looks,” but offered praise to the Senate hopeful as “the greatest” attorney general in the country.

“I don’t know if he’s gonna ever speak to me again, but you know, I don’t care as long as he wins,” Trump said. “I don’t have to speak to him. He’s gonna vote the way we would vote … you gotta vote for him.”

The president’s closing-night speech echoed many of his first-night points, including the digs at Paxton. But he hammered a critical throughline pushed by many of the convention’s speakers: that the midterms are an existential fight for the GOP.

“They’ll ruin our country. So on election day, November 3, you got to do me a favor. You got to get out and vote, and you’re going to pretend I’m on the ballot because, in a way, I am on the ballot,” Trump said.

He went on to lead the crowd in a pledge to turn out in November’s general election. At the end, he said that those who don’t vote will “go to hell.”

Vance will not stray far from the spotlight following the convention.

He’ll travel to New York City on Friday for a commemorating the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terror attacks at Ground Zero alongside former presidents. And he’s headed next week to Kansas City, Missouri, where he’ll deliver remarks on the Trump administration’s efforts to combat fraud.
